title: Evaluation, calibration & experimental design
summary: Make model comparisons that survive contact with real data and actual decisions.
html:
Make model comparisons that survive contact with real data and actual decisions.

Separate fitting from selection

Use training data to fit parameters, validation data to choose models and thresholds, and a held-out test for the final comparison. Repeatedly optimizing against a test set effectively turns it into validation data. Cross-validation helps estimate variability, provided folds respect groups and time.

Metrics answer different questions

Precision asks how many predicted positives were positive. Recall asks how many actual positives were found. PR curves are often informative for rare events. AUROC evaluates ranking across thresholds but can look strong while precision is poor. For regression, MAE and RMSE penalize errors differently.

Calibrated confidence

Among predictions near 0.8, calibration asks whether roughly 80% are correct under the specified event definition. Reliability diagrams, Brier score, and log loss help assess probability quality. Recalibration uses held-out data and can fail under distribution shift.

Measure the system and its slices

Report sample counts, uncertainty, baselines, and important subgroups. Paired comparisons on the same examples can reduce variance. Online experiments need assignment units that avoid interference. Evaluate fallback behavior, cost, response time, and human correction work alongside model quality.

Worked example

A classifier yields 80 true positives, 20 false positives, and 40 false negatives. Precision=80/100=0.80; recall=80/120≈0.667; F1≈0.727. Neither metric alone says whether the system is acceptable without error costs and population context.

What goes wrong

An improvement smaller than run-to-run variation may be noise. Selecting the best of many trials without accounting for selection makes gains look more reliable than they are.

Check your understanding

Why is a customer-grouped split sometimes better than a random row split?

Reveal the explanation

It tests generalization to new customers rather than recognition of repeated patterns from customers already seen in training.

How the pieces connect

A usable chapter has a flow of decisions, evidence, and checks. Use this diagram as a navigation aid, then test each step on a small real example.

An operating model for evaluation, calibration & experimental design

Evaluation is an experiment design problem. The test set estimates behavior under the world your split represents. If deployment is temporal, grouped, adversarial, multilingual, or costly, a random aggregate score cannot answer the whole question. Measurement needs to follow the actual decision path.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Field guide: four decisions in order

1. Specify outcome

Specify outcome establishes the next constraint. Name the user decision and target population. Begin by making the object of study explicit. A vague input, target, or operating condition creates ambiguity that later computation cannot repair.

Write down the input boundary and the unit of analysis. This makes it possible to distinguish a missing fact from a mismatch between the question and the data or system.

2. Design split

Design split establishes the next constraint. Protect held-out data from all selection steps. Now make the mechanism inspectable. Prefer a small run whose intermediate values, examples, or traces can be examined before you automate a larger workflow.

Keep a concrete artifact: a small dataset, a notebook cell, a trace, a benchmark command, or a hand-worked calculation. It is the fastest way to surface hidden assumptions.

3. Measure

Measure establishes the next constraint. Use metrics, uncertainty, and slices. Treat the first result as a measurement, not a conclusion. Compare it with a baseline and vary one assumption at a time so that the observed change has an interpretable cause.

Check a deliberately awkward case alongside the happy path. Boundary conditions, rare examples, and resource limits reveal more than another aggregate score.

4. Decide

Decide establishes the next constraint. Compare against baseline and operational constraints. Finish by connecting the result to a real choice. Record the operating range, uncertainty, and the condition under which the next person should stop, escalate, or revisit the earlier steps.

Preserve the decision record with the result. A useful technical chapter leaves enough context for a reader to reproduce the reasoning, challenge it, and choose a safe next action.

When the first approach fails

Do not respond to a weak result by immediately adding scale, complexity, or another framework. First locate the failure: the input may not match the intended problem; the representation may discard a useful signal; the measurement may reward the wrong outcome; or the system may have crossed a memory, latency, reliability, or authority boundary. Change one layer, repeat the smallest useful check, and keep the before-and-after evidence.

Gotcha. A polished output can hide an untested assumption. The most convincing demonstration is a counterexample the workflow handles deliberately, with the limitation stated in the release or research record.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Specify outcome. Name the user decision and target population.
  2. Design split. Protect held-out data from all selection steps.
  3. Measure. Use metrics, uncertainty, and slices.
  4. Decide. Compare against baseline and operational constraints.

Create an evaluation card for every release: data version, split rule, sample size, baselines, metric definitions, confidence intervals, slices, latency, cost, and known blind spots.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
